c.tagline: Coffee, grunge and evergreen — a tech city wedged between the mountains and the sea.

taxi.fareNote: Metered taxis start around $2.60 plus about $2.70 per mile; most visitors use Uber or Lyft, which are widely available. Flat-rate fares apply on some Sea-Tac Airport trips.

emergency.note: 911 is the single nationwide number that reaches police, fire, and ambulance.

english.label: Easy to get by in English

avoid.reason: Caution around 3rd Ave, Pioneer Square and parts of downtown at night — drug activity/property crime

hood_desc: Seattle's walkable core, home to Pike Place Market, the waterfront, the Seattle Art Museum, and the main retail district; the most convenient base for first-timers who want major sights and transit at their doorstep.

The city's nightlife and LGBTQ+ heart, packed with bars, live-music venues, indie coffee shops, and restaurants along the Pike/Pine corridor; best for travelers who want to stay out late and eat well.
A dense downtown neighborhood of high-rises, cocktail bars, and restaurants a short walk from the Space Needle and Seattle Center; good for nightlife and dining close to the action.

A former Scandinavian fishing town turned trendy northwest neighborhood, known for craft breweries, its Sunday farmers market, seafood spots, and the Ballard Locks; suits visitors wanting a hip, local feel.
A quirky, self-proclaimed 'Center of the Universe' with the Fremont Troll, vintage shops, canal-side breweries, and a laid-back arty vibe; good for offbeat, indie exploring.

water.note: Tap water from Cascade watersheds is safe and tastes good.

transit.pay: Tap an ORCA card (or a contactless bank card or phone on most services) when you board. Link light rail is a flat $3 adult fare; King County Metro buses are $2.75 and the Seattle Streetcar is $2.25. An ORCA card costs $3, and an all-day regional pass is about $6. On Link you tap on and tap off; on buses you tap on only.
transit.hours: Link light rail runs roughly 5am to 1am (later on Friday and Saturday); buses vary, with several 24-hour and Night Owl routes. Washington State Ferries run from early morning until late at night.

transit.m: Link 1 Line light rail to downtown (~38 min)
Sound Transit Express bus to downtown

tip.r: ~15-20% at sit-down restaurants; $1-2 per drink at bars and a couple of dollars for taxis and porters.

food.name: Dungeness crab
food.desc: Sweet, meaty Pacific Northwest crab, served cracked and cold with drawn butter, in a mayo-dressed roll, or folded into chowder.

places.name: Local Tide
places.note: Acclaimed Dungeness crab roll with lemon and chives; go early, they sell out.

places.name: Pike Place Chowder
places.note: Award-winning Dungeness crab and smoked salmon chowders; expect a line worth joining.

places.name: Cutter's Crabhouse
places.note: Big Elliott Bay views with whole crab, crab Louie and a solid happy hour.

food.name: Seattle-style teriyaki
food.desc: A local fast-food genre born here in the 1970s: charcoal-grilled marinated chicken thigh over rice with a sweet-salty glaze and a scoop of green salad.

places.name: Toshi's Teriyaki Grill
places.note: Toshi Kasahara invented Seattle teriyaki in 1976 and is still the reference point.

places.name: Nikko Teriyaki
places.note: Repeatedly named among the state's best; generous portions, great char on the chicken.

places.name: Teriyaki Madness
places.note: Quick, cheap and reliable when you want the standard version close to downtown.

food.name: Wild Pacific salmon
food.desc: King, sockeye or coho, often alder-planked over an open fire the way Coast Salish peoples cooked it, or smoked and stirred into chowder.

places.name: Ivar's Salmon House
places.note: Alder-grilled salmon in a longhouse-style room with float-plane and skyline views.

places.name: Ivar's Acres of Clams
places.note: Seattle institution for wild Alaskan salmon and cup-of-chowder-on-the-pier tradition.

places.name: RockCreek Seafood and Spirits
places.note: Chef-driven, sustainability-focused seafood; the salmon changes with the run.

food.name: Seattle dog
food.desc: The city's late-night street dog: a grilled frank in a bun schmeared with cream cheese, then piled with grilled onions and often sriracha or jalapenos.

places.name: Dante's Inferno Dogs
places.note: Perfected the Seattle dog and even built a cream cheese gun; Sundays in Ballard.

places.name: Monster Dogs
places.note: Classic sidewalk cart at bar-closing time, exactly how the Seattle dog is meant to be eaten.

food.name: Puget Sound oysters
food.desc: Kumamoto, Shigoku and Olympia oysters pulled from cold local tidelands, shucked to order and eaten raw with mignonette.

places.name: The Walrus and the Carpenter
places.note: James Beard-winning small raw bar; the room that made Seattle an oyster town again.

places.name: Taylor Shellfish Oyster Bar
places.note: Owned by a fifth-generation shellfish farm, so the oysters are as direct as it gets.

places.name: Elliott's Oyster House
places.note: Enormous rotating oyster list on Pier 56, with a sliding-scale happy hour.

food.name: Seattle espresso
food.desc: The city that gave the world the latte still takes it seriously: dark, syrupy shots, thick microfoam and latte art invented locally.

places.name: Espresso Vivace
places.note: David Schomer popularized American latte art here; the classic Seattle espresso profile.

places.name: Victrola Coffee Roasters
places.note: Neighborhood roastery with free Wednesday cuppings and consistently excellent shots.

places.name: Storyville Coffee
places.note: Warm loft space above the market with rooftop views over Elliott Bay.

food.name: Washington craft beer
food.desc: Yakima Valley grows a large share of America's hops, and Seattle's breweries pour the results as crisp pilsners and resinous Northwest IPAs.

places.name: Fremont Brewing
places.note: Open-air Urban Beer Garden, family and dog friendly; Interurban IPA is the local pour.

places.name: Holy Mountain Brewing
places.note: Small, highly rated brewery known for saisons and barrel-aged and mixed-fermentation beers.

places.name: Cloudburst Brewing
places.note: No-nonsense taproom steps from the market with constantly rotating hoppy releases.

landmarks: Space Needle
The 605-foot 1962 World's Fair tower is Seattle's most recognizable silhouette and a classic skyline photo subject.
Pike Place Market
The historic 1907 public market with its neon clock and fish-throwing vendors is one of the most photographed scenes in the city.
Chihuly Garden and Glass
Dale Chihuly's vivid glass sculptures set against the Space Needle make for striking, colorful compositions.
Kerry Park
This small hillside park offers the quintessential postcard view of the Space Needle framed by downtown and Mount Rainier.
Gas Works Park
The rusting industrial gasification towers on Lake Union create a surreal foreground for skyline sunset shots.
Museum of Pop Culture (MoPOP)
Frank Gehry's swirling, colorful metallic building is one of the most architecturally striking structures in Seattle Center.
Seattle Great Wheel
The illuminated waterfront Ferris wheel on Pier 57 lights up Elliott Bay at night for dramatic long-exposure shots.
Pioneer Square
Seattle's oldest neighborhood, with Victorian-era brick buildings and totem poles, offers historic architectural charm.
Fremont Troll
This whimsical giant troll sculpture crushing a VW Beetle under the Aurora Bridge is a quirky, must-photograph oddity.
Smith Tower
Once the tallest building on the West Coast, this 1914 terracotta skyscraper offers a rooftop observatory view of the city.

train.note: King Street Station, just south of downtown by Pioneer Square, handles everything. Two Amtrak Cascades round trips a day run north to Vancouver, British Columbia in about 4 hours, while the rest of the Cascades fleet works south to Portland in 3.5 hours and on to Eugene. The Coast Starlight runs daily to Portland, Sacramento and Los Angeles, and the Empire Builder heads east to Spokane, Glacier National Park and Chicago. Southbound from Canada, passengers now clear US formalities at Vancouver's Pacific Central Station, which in June 2026 became North America's first rail preclearance facility; northbound checks happen on arrival, so carry a passport and allow extra time.

bus.note: Intercity coaches use the terminal at 503 S Royal Brougham Way in SoDo, a short walk from King Street Station, plus curbside stops nearby. FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/) run the I-5 corridor south to Portland in 3.5-4 hours and north through Bellingham to Vancouver BC in about 4. Older operators such as BoltBus and Quick Shuttle no longer run, so ignore out-of-date listings that still name them. Everyone gets off the coach at the Peace Arch or Pacific Highway crossing for Canadian immigration, which can add an hour at busy times; Amtrak Thruway buses also cover the Vancouver run when Cascades trains are disrupted.

intl.to: Victoria, BC (Canada) - passenger-only catamaran from Pier 69 downtown
Victoria, BC (Canada) - car ferry from Port Angeles, about 2.5 hours west of Seattle
Bainbridge Island, Bremerton & the Kitsap Peninsula (USA) - from Colman Dock, Pier 52

ferry.note: The Victoria Clipper is the only direct international boat, a foot-passenger catamaran from Pier 69 to Victoria's Inner Harbour taking under three hours, year-round with more sailings in summer - book ahead and allow 45-60 minutes for check-in and customs. With a car you use the MV Coho from Port Angeles instead, a 90-minute crossing where vehicle space should be reserved well in advance. Washington State Ferries sail constantly from Colman Dock in the middle of downtown to Bainbridge Island (35 minutes) and Bremerton (about an hour); walk-on passengers simply turn up, but vehicles queue at peak times. The international Anacortes-Sidney BC route has been suspended since 2020 and is not expected to return before 2030.

half.name: Snoqualmie Falls
half.blurb: A 268-foot waterfall on the Snoqualmie River with a viewing platform, about half an hour east of the city.

half.name: Bainbridge Island
half.blurb: A short ferry ride across Puget Sound to a wooded island town of galleries, gardens, and waterfront trails.

half.name: Whidbey Island
half.blurb: An island reached by ferry with waterfront towns, state parks, and views across the Salish Sea to the Olympic Mountains.

full.name: Mount Rainier National Park
full.blurb: An active volcano and the state's highest peak, with old-growth forest trails, wildflower meadows, and glacier-fed rivers.

full.name: Leavenworth
full.blurb: A Bavarian-themed alpine village in the Cascades with timber-frame architecture, built around a former railroad and timber town.
